title: Be the valley
hook: know the strong, keep to the soft, and be the valley of the world (Tao Te Ching 28)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-seven, and your line was no tracks. Did you leave a place better, with nobody watching? How did it feel to get no credit? Day one thousand ninety.

From the top of a ridge, the whole landscape seems to be leaning one way. Streams run down. Paths wind down. Birds drop down into the trees below. Down there, at the bottom, is the valley, and everything ends up in it: the water, the soil, the green, the people who built the village along the river. The peak gets the view. The valley gets the life. Chapter twenty-eight of the Tao Te Ching asks a person to choose the valley on purpose, while knowing full well what it's like to stand on the peak.
screen: `FROM THE TOP OF A RIDGE.` → `EVERYTHING RUNS DOWN.` → `THE VALLEY GETS THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, know the strong, keep to the soft. The chapter opens with a pair. In the Chinese, the words are male and female. Know the male, it says, but keep to the female. Some readers hear in the pair the strong and the soft. The point is not to be ignorant of strength. You know exactly what it is. You just don't live from there. Second, the valley of the world. Do that, the chapter says, and you become the stream-bed of the world, the low channel everything runs into. Later it says the same with another word: the valley of the world. Low, open, receiving. As with the ridge and the valley a moment ago, the high place is admired, but the low place is where things gather. Third, back to infant, back to uncarved. Then the chapter reaches back. It says that whoever is the stream-bed of the world returns to being an infant, and whoever is the valley returns to the uncarved block. Those are two pictures we've already met: drifting like an infant, eight days ago, and the plain uncarved wood, nine days ago. Here the book ties them together. The soft way leads back to the beginning. Fourth, great carving doesn't cut. The chapter ends with the uncarved block split up into useful vessels, and the sage, put to use, becoming a leader of officials. And then a final line, which some translators render as: the great carver does not cut. The best shaping, in this picture, leaves the thing whole.
screen: `KNOW THE STRONG, KEEP THE SOFT.` · `THE VALLEY OF THE WORLD.` · `BACK TO INFANT, BACK TO UNCARVED.` · `GREAT CARVING DOESN'T CUT.` · then, large: `BE THE VALLEY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the soft way once. Settle, and let your shoulders drop, the way water runs downhill. Bring to mind one place today where you could push: an argument, a deadline, a person who's slow. You know how to be strong there. Now picture the soft way instead: a lower voice, an open question, a moment of making room. You're not giving up your strength. You're choosing not to lead with it. Hold that picture while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Be the valley. Chapter twenty-eight's picture of a person who knows strength and keeps to softness, low and open, where everything gathers. Today's word.
Your line: be the valley. When you could push today, choose the soft way once, and notice what flows toward you instead. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-eight as a way of carrying strength: knowing how to be forceful, and choosing receptiveness and humility instead.

myth: chapter twenty-eight says to stay ignorant of strength
it says know the strong, and keep to the soft. you know it; you just don't live from there.
the chapter ties the valley back to the infant and the uncarved block
the stream-bed of the world returns to the infant; the valley of the world returns to the uncarved block.
the chapter ends by praising the carver who cuts the most
its last line, as some translators render it: the great carver does not cut.

fork.setup: you know how to be strong, and you could win this one by pushing. you're reading chapter twenty-eight. what does it ask?
options: pretend you have no strength at all.
know the strong, and keep to the soft.
fork.reveal: know the male, keep to the female, and be the valley of the world: low, open, the place everything runs to.

original.note: Chinese, wéi tiānxià xī: be the stream-valley of the world, from Tao Te Ching 28.

trapdoor: what you thought: be the valley means be a pushover.
what it means: know strength, keep to softness, and be the low, open place everything runs into.
what a scholar hears: xi and gu, two words for valley, and a chapter that returns to the infant and the uncarved block, pu, and ends: great carving does not cut.

notes: Chapter 28 is paraphrased throughout. The middle stanza (know the white, keep to the black, be the pattern of the world, return to the limitless) is left out for length.
The opening pair 雄/雌 is given as 'male and female', with a note that the outline renders it 'strong and soft'. Confirm this is fair and not over-gendered for the listener.
谿 (xī, stream-valley/ravine) and 谷 (gǔ, valley) are both rendered in the teach; 'stream-bed of the world' is used for 谿. Confirm.
'大制不割' is given as 'the great carver does not cut', attributed to 'some translators'; this is an interpretive rendering ('great cutting does not sever').
The teach refers back to day 1082 (drifting like an infant, 'eight days ago') and day 1081 (the uncarved block, 'nine days ago'); counts checked against day numbers.
The ridge-and-valley scene is an illustration, not a source.
Pronunciation guide for 為天下谿 is approximate.

Editor: removed 'our outline puts it as' (internal planning language spoken to the listener) in favor of 'some readers hear'; split the returns correctly (stream-bed returns to the infant, valley to the uncarved block, as the chapter's stanzas do); replaced 'does something lovely' (narrator uplift) and the 'in the hook' reference; recast the ruler line closer to Legge (the sage employed becomes head of the officers); changed the practice's low-belly breath, which repeated day 1088.
